evidence_quotes.quote: We analysed data from 593 households in Mandala, a slum with legally recognized (notified) and unrecognized (non-notified) neighbourhoods.

To prove they meet notification requirements, households must have an official document, such as a voter ID card, dated before 2000. Those without such documentation are barred from receiving municipal services and have no right to rehabilitation.

To understand the independent effect of legal status, we conducted multivariate regression analyses with water quantity used by households, in litres per capita per day (LPCD), as the outcome of interest.
Median water cost for notified households was 219 Indian rupees (INR)/1000 litres, while non-notified households paid a median of 407 INR/1000 litres (USD2.92 and 5.42, respectively).
Non-notified households used 37 per cent fewer LPCD on average than notified households, which translates to 12 fewer LPCD based on median water quantity used by notified households.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water service access (and also reports household sanitation access in Table 1) in Mandala, an urban slum in Mumbai, India.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies Criterion 2 under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines a legal and administrative factor (legal recognition / slum notification status). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly analyses rule-type mechanisms governing municipal water service access: legal eligibility rules under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act of 1971, pre-2000 residence cut-off documentation requirements (e.g. voter ID card), state vs. central government land-tenure rules, group application requirements for municipal community water taps, and municipal officials' discretion in operationalizing notification at neighbourhood vs. household levels.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains quantitative primary empirical evidence from a representative cross-sectional household survey (N = 593 analysed of 600 randomly sampled households) combined with GIS mapping of community water taps, multivariate linear and logistic regression, and GSEM path analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple household-level water access outcomes, including primary and secondary modes of water access (in-home tap, shared community tap/tank, informal hose vendor, tanker truck), tap functionality via GIS mapping, collection time and source crowding, supply reliability, water quantity consumed (litres per capita per day and <=20 LPCD threshold), and affordability/cost (INR per 1,000 litres and share of monthly household income spent on water), alongside basic sanitation access in Table 1.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and unit of analysis (593 households across notified Matangrushi Nagar [n = 283] and non-notified Indira Nagar [n = 310] in Mandala slum, Mumbai), exposure (legal status: non-notified vs. notified status governing municipal water eligibility), outcomes (water quantity in LPCD, access modes, reliability, time, and cost), and study design (cross-sectional representative household survey with GIS mapping, multivariate regression, and path analysis; also provides sufficient statistical information for quantitative effect extraction).

study_design: Cross-sectional representative household survey with GIS infrastructure mapping, multivariate linear and logistic regression, and GSEM path analysis
population_and_sample: 593 randomly sampled households (283 in notified Matangrushi Nagar and 310 in non-notified Indira Nagar; 600 surveyed, 7 excluded due to missing water variables) in Mandala urban slum, M-East ward, Mumbai, India; unit of analysis is the household (with GIS mapping of community water taps)
exposure: Legal recognition (notification vs. non-notified legal status under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act of 1971, pre-2000 documentation requirements, and neighbourhood-level operationalization of municipal service eligibility)
outcome: Household water service access indicators: water quantity consumed (litres per capita per day and <=20 LPCD), primary and secondary modes of water access (in-home tap, community tap, vendor hose, tanker truck), GIS-mapped tap functionality, collection time and source crowding, weekly supply reliability and days with insufficient water, water cost (INR/1000L and percentage of monthly household income), and household sanitation method (Table 1)
rationale: This empirical quantitative study directly evaluates how legal exclusion (non-notified vs. notified legal status under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act, pre-2000 documentation rules, and municipal application/discretion rules) shapes household water access, infrastructure availability, reliability, cost, and quantity (LPCD) across 593 randomly sampled slum households in Mumbai, India. All inclusion criteria (c1-c6) are clearly satisfied under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2, and quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported.
